title: State, Identity, and the Cost of Uncertainty
html:
A retry looks harmless when the operation only reads data. It may consume another database connection or add more work to an overloaded service, but it does not normally change the record being read. A payment authorization is different. The provider can accept the first request even if its response never reaches Baodium. Sending a second, independent authorization can reserve the customer’s money twice.

During a Black Friday at Baodium, a customer clicked Pay, waited for a confirmation that never appeared, and tried again. Baodium stored one order, but the payment provider recorded two authorizations, and the customer saw two pending payment entries.

The two authorizations came from the absence of a durable identity linking the customer’s attempts to one intended purchase. The recovery procedure also lacked reliable evidence of what the provider had done. Inventory reservations and shipment requests present the same class of problem: a repeated call can reserve stock twice or dispatch another parcel when an earlier result was never confirmed.

Payment Outcomes After Timeout

When the provider request times out, Checkout has recorded only that no response arrived before the deadline. The request might never have reached the provider. The provider might have rejected it, with the response lost on the way back. It might have completed the authorization, or it might still be processing the request.

Checkout’s records are identical in all four cases, showing a submitted request and no response. The next action has to be safe in every one of them. The customer sees the same missing confirmation in each case, although the appropriate next step depends on the provider’s result. Authorization reserves funds for a payment, so another independent authorization can reserve funds again. Capture, which may happen later, collects the authorized funds.

In Baodium’s incident, the provider had completed the first authorization. Checkout recorded failure because it had not received the response, then submitted an independent authorization when the customer retried. Checkout’s database contained no record of the provider’s remote outcome. Its transaction controlled the local order and payment records, while the provider committed its records separately. Rolling back a local transaction could not remove the authorization the provider had already completed.

The revised handler recorded an unresolved outcome when it could not confirm the result. The page explained that payment was being verified and checked the existing order for updates. Another click on Pay retrieved the same payment operation.

Disabling the Pay button reduced accidental clicks, but a retrying client library or another browser session could still submit the request. Recognizing those submissions was therefore part of the server’s payment logic. To implement this, checkout needed a durable record of the authorization it intended to perform. That record had to exist before the provider call, since the handler could stop immediately after sending the request.

Operation, Record, and Message Identity

Checkout uses three separate identities.

Identities used in the checkout workflow.
Identity What it identifies Example use
Record ID A stored business entity. Retrieve an order and its payment history.
Operation ID One intended business action. Recognize repeated attempts to authorize the same payment.
Message ID One published event. Recognize repeated delivery before applying a local update.

An order ID identifies the purchase, and that purchase can have several payment operations, including authorization, capture, and refund. Each needs its own identity so the application can distinguish a repeated attempt from a new action.

For instance, retrying an authorization after a lost response uses the original operation ID. Refunding part of that payment creates another operation ID linked to the payment. A later partial refund receives its own ID, even if its amount matches the earlier refund.

A provider may support idempotent requests, using an idempotency key to recognize repeated submissions of the same business operation. Without that guarantee, sending a payment request again can create a second authorization. Baodium durably associates its operation ID with the key sent to the provider, so recovery uses the same identity as the original attempt. The provider’s API contract determines how long the key remains valid, what fields must match, and whether a retry from another region receives the original result.

Message identity becomes relevant when a service publishes an event through a broker. The producer assigns an ID when it creates the event and preserves that ID across publication attempts. A consumer can then recognize an event it has already processed. We will use this distinction in the outbox section.

During support investigations, these relationships allow an engineer to start with an order, find its payment operations, and retrieve the provider references. Storing the mapping in durable records makes recovery independent of whether the original request logs are still available.

A Durable Payment Operation

Baodium’s revised checkout stored the authorization intent before calling the provider. The record described the action to perform and provided a place for its outcome. If the process crashes after dispatch, another handler can inspect the record to determine whether an attempt was made, which identity was used, and what evidence is still required before retrying.

Here, 10000 represents $100 in the currency’s minor units. Checkout obtained the amount and currency from the server-side order record. The payment-method reference was a provider token, so the operation contained no raw card details.

The provider authorization ID was initially empty because the provider had not yet returned one. The operation ID was already available, and every submission used its associated provider key. If the handler stopped after committing this record, another handler could recover the intended action without reconstructing it from browser input. Recovery used the recorded payment details, even if other order or customer information had subsequently changed.

Repeated Requests and Conflicting Details

Suppose a caller requests an authorization for $100, then repeats the same key with an amount of $1,000. Returning the first result would conceal the conflict, while submitting the new amount could create an unintended payment. Checkout therefore rejects the conflicting request before contacting the provider.

Baodium compared the fields that defined the operation, including the order, amount, currency, payment-method reference, operation type, and provider account. These values could be compared directly or through a fingerprint calculated from normalized fields. Attempt numbers and tracing headers were excluded because they can change between retries. If fingerprints are used, their normalization rules need a version so a deployment can still interpret operations created by earlier code.

A matching request can retrieve the recorded outcome or pending status, subject to the caller’s permission to access the order. Possession of an idempotency key grants no additional access. A browser might also generate a new key when the customer clicks Pay again. Checking keys alone would allow another authorization for the unresolved purchase; preventing that requires a rule about the order itself.

Concurrent Submissions

Two submissions can reach checkout together and both observe an unpaid order. If each handler checks the order and inserts a payment operation independently, both can create an authorization. A sequential test may pass because the second handler sees the first handler’s committed operation. Concurrent submissions can both pass the initial check before either has inserted a record. A transaction and uniqueness rule must prevent them from creating separate payment operations.

Baodium serialized this decision in a local database transaction. The handler locked the order record, checked its current payment operation, and either retrieved that operation or created a new one when the order’s payment state permitted it. All paths that could initiate payment used this procedure.

The operation and the order’s reference to it committed together. A concurrent submission then found the existing operation, including when the browser supplied a new key. Conflicting payment details were rejected using the comparison described earlier.

The transaction ended before the provider call, and its database connection was released. Checkout then sent the stored identity and payment details.

Two handlers might still submit the same operation if a retry overlaps the original call, and both use the same provider key. The order-level check prevents independent authorizations for an unresolved payment, while provider idempotency handles repeated submissions of the selected operation.

Provider Guarantees

That last step depends on what the provider guarantees. A local operation record cannot prevent an external service from performing the same write twice. The engineers checked the key’s scope, the treatment of concurrent submissions, the available recovery methods, and the retention period for duplicate recognition. A key may be scoped to a particular account or operation type, so recovery must use the corresponding account and endpoint.

A provider might support lookup by operation key, retrieval of a durable payment object, or another submission using the original key. Some APIs return an in-progress or conflict response when matching requests overlap. Checkout needs to handle that response without creating a replacement authorization.

These details belong in the integration contract because they determine the available recovery actions. If the provider offers no way to deduplicate or resolve an interrupted write, another recovery channel is required, potentially involving an operator.

Recording the Outcome

A confirmed authorization allowed checkout to record success, and a definitive decline allowed it to record failure. The handler also had to account for interruptions before it could save either result.

Recovery information available after an interruption.
Interruption Recovery information
Before the local intent commits No provider call is permitted. A repeated request can create or retrieve the intent.
After intent commit, before submission A pending operation exists. Recovery uses its stored identity.
After provider authorization, before local result commit The local operation is unresolved. Recovery obtains provider evidence.
After local result commit, before the browser receives it A repeated request retrieves the recorded result.

The second and third rows can look identical locally. In both cases, a recovery worker may find a pending operation with no provider reference. A submitted flag cannot eliminate this gap. The process could stop between updating the flag and sending the request, or between sending the request and updating the flag.

The worker therefore uses the original operation identity to obtain provider evidence; it cannot infer the outcome from the local pending record. Baodium’s background process examined operations explicitly marked for reconciliation and pending operations that had passed their expected processing period. Scanning both covered process failures that never reached an exception handler.

Once the result was confirmed, the operation update and corresponding order transition committed in one local transaction. The record included the provider reference, when available, and the evidence used to establish the outcome. Subsequent requests could retrieve that result.

State Transitions and Delayed Results

The payment operation describes one action; the order describes checkout progress, which also depends on inventory, fulfillment, and cancellation. An authorization can succeed while checkout is still waiting for another step. Figure Figure shows the payment-related order states and their transitions.

Baodium used the following order states for the payment portion of checkout.

Payment-related order states. Each operation also retains its identity, outcome, and provider evidence.
Order state Meaning for checkout
PENDING_PAYMENT Payment has not been confirmed. Any submitted authorization has an attached operation record.
RECONCILIATION_PENDING The authorization requires recovery. An independent replacement authorization is blocked.
PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED Authorization is confirmed. Checkout can continue according to its inventory policy.
PAYMENT_FAILED The current authorization has a definitive unsuccessful outcome.
MANUAL_REVIEW Recovery requires an operator. An unresolved payment still blocks an independent replacement.

For example, a definitive decline may allow the customer to choose another payment method. The new authorization receives another operation ID, while the earlier operation is preserved in the payment history. The order identifies which operation is current.

Now consider a recovery worker that reads the order, contacts the provider, and receives a response after another handler has updated checkout. Applying that result using only the order ID could overwrite newer progress. Checking only the state name is insufficient too; an order can enter a payment-pending state again for a later operation. Baodium therefore checked the current operation ID, expected state, and record version before updating the order.

Every order update increments the version. If another handler has changed the record since the worker read it, the expected version no longer matches. This statement belongs in the transaction that records the operation’s confirmed result. If it updates zero rows, the handler rolls back that attempted transaction and reloads the records before deciding what to do. Another worker may already have recorded the same result. The order may have progressed for another valid reason, or the provider evidence may conflict with an earlier result. Unexpected evidence is preserved for investigation.

A cancellation during payment processing illustrates why this check matters. A late authorization may require a void, so the handler must record the provider result through a recovery path appropriate to the canceled order. It must not resume ordinary checkout merely because authorization succeeded.

Decision review

The status lookup says NOT_FOUND

A payment authorization timed out four minutes ago. The operation record is in RECONCILIATION_PENDING . A recovery worker calls the provider’s status endpoint with the operation identifier and receives NOT_FOUND. The customer is waiting, and support has asked whether they can retry the purchase.

Treat NOT_FOUND as proof that no authorization exists, mark the operation failed, and let the customer try again.

Submit the original request again under the same idempotency key.

Leave the operation unresolved and retry the lookup after a delay, escalating to manual review at the recovery deadline.

A requires a provider guarantee that NOT_FOUND rules out both a completed authorization and an original request that could still commit. Without that guarantee, the original request might complete after the lookup. A new purchase could then create a second authorization and reserve the customer’s funds twice.

B depends on the provider’s idempotency contract. The original key must still be recognized, the request must match the original operation, and a repeat must not create a second authorization. The provider may complete the original operation or return its recorded result. Section Section lists the contract details. If local records are retained for fourteen days but provider keys for seven, the local record alone does not make a repeat safe after key expiry.

C preserves the unresolved state without submitting another authorization, which is the supported action while those provider guarantees are unknown. The recovery deadline assigns the case to an operator if the lookup cannot establish the outcome. The cost is a longer pending purchase, which the customer and support need to be able to track.

Provider Reconciliation

Consider the position of a recovery worker that wakes up holding an unresolved payment. Everything it is permitted to do follows from what it can prove.

Reconciliation resolves a local operation against provider evidence. It may use a status lookup, an authenticated provider notification, or a repeated request covered by the provider’s idempotency contract. Three details need particular care when implementing it: the meaning of a missing result, the period during which a request can be repeated, and ownership of recovery work.

Interpreting a Missing Result

A response such as NOT_FOUND can appear to settle the question, but its meaning depends on the lookup contract. For instance, the original request may still be processing when a recovery worker asks for its result. The lookup finds no completed authorization, then the original request commits; creating a replacement after that lookup could produce two authorizations.

We treat “not found” as a statement about the lookup rather than about the world. It means only that the provider had no completed record at that instant. Before treating absence as a definitive unsuccessful outcome, checkout needs an authoritative lookup and assurance that the earlier attempt cannot complete later. A searchable history covering several days does not, by itself, provide those guarantees.

Where the provider permits another submission with the same key and identical parameters, recovery can use that protocol. Otherwise, the operation needs further reconciliation or operator review.

Retention and Recovery Deadlines

Local operation records need to cover the period during which delayed jobs, callbacks, recovery workers, or operators can repeat an action. Provider retention needs a separate check. Suppose Baodium retains operation records for fourteen days, but the provider recognizes duplicate keys for seven. On day eight, a worker can read the original key, yet submitting it may create another authorization. Recovery after that point needs durable provider evidence or an operator procedure. Before sending an old queued request, the worker checks whether the provider still guarantees duplicate recognition for that operation.

These periods are illustrative. An integration needs the provider’s actual guarantees, including any difference between retention of idempotency keys and payment records. The payment may still be retrievable after its request key has expired.

Local deletion also needs a policy. If an old request arrives after its deduplication record has been removed, the application might treat it as new. Depending on the business workflow, the application can retain a smaller record of the final outcome or reject expired operations using a server-issued identity with an enforced validity period.

An escalation deadline determines when an operator becomes responsible for an unresolved case. Passing that deadline provides no additional evidence about whether authorization succeeded.

Recovery Workers

A background worker usually claims an operation for a limited period before processing it. This claim, often called a lease, reduces overlapping work while allowing another worker to continue after a process failure. Baodium stored an owner token and expiry time with each claim, and renewals and result updates checked both the token and the claim’s validity. A worker with an expired claim could no longer update the record through that claim.

You may wonder why the token is needed when the expiry already limits the claim. The reason is the worker that stalls. If it wakes up after its lease has expired and another worker has taken over, the token is what stops it from overwriting the newer worker’s result.

It might still receive a late provider response. Expiring a local claim does not cancel a request executing remotely, so a replacement worker must use the same operation identity and provider recovery protocol.

Batch size matters as well. A worker that claims many records and processes them sequentially may not reach the later records before their claims expire. Claiming work as processing capacity becomes available reduces that overlap.

Synchronous responses, recovery workers, and provider notifications used the same guarded result-recording procedure. Notifications were authenticated and matched to the stored operation, account, and payment details before they affected checkout.

Compensation After Partial Completion

Payments have an awkward property: they can succeed on their own while the purchase around them collapses.

Checkout also needs a response when payment succeeds but a later step cannot complete. Inventory may be unavailable, or the customer may cancel before fulfillment begins.

Compensation is a business action that counteracts an earlier effect, and the appropriate action depends on what has already happened.

Compensation performs another business action. After a captured payment, a refund creates a credit linked to the original charge. Both can appear in the payment history, and fees depend on the provider’s contract. Canceling a shipment may require a carrier request, and an email already delivered cannot be recalled by rolling back a local transaction. The recovery procedure therefore needs the business outcome each corrective action can achieve.

The business owner must therefore approve the compensating action before it becomes an automated recovery rule. Releasing a reservation or refunding a payment may each be technically possible, but releasing stock after a merchant has packed the order could contradict the agreed fulfillment policy. Engineers are well placed to enumerate which states are reachable. They are not well placed to decide what the company should do about each one.

Compensation depends on the current business state and the receiving service’s contract.
Confirmed effect Possible counteraction
Uncaptured authorization Void or cancel the authorization.
Captured payment Refund the permitted amount.
Inventory reservation Release that reservation.
Fulfillment request Cancel if fulfillment has not passed the cancellation point.

Consider an authorization followed by a definitive inventory rejection; Checkout needs to void the uncaptured authorization. The void receives its own operation ID and provider key, and its stored details identify the authorization being voided.

Baodium created the compensation operation and changed the order to COMPENSATION_PENDING in one local transaction. A worker then processed that existing operation. If the process stopped after the transaction, another worker could find the pending void and continue.

A confirmed void completed that payment counteraction; a lost response required reconciliation of the void. A definitive provider refusal could place the case in COMPENSATION_FAILED , with an operator assigned to investigate. If capture had occurred, the next action might be a refund based on the confirmed payment state.

The inventory result can also be uncertain; a timeout may mean a reservation exists anyway. Before declaring checkout fully compensated, the application must resolve that operation and release any reservation it created. Recovery can involve several outstanding actions for one order.

Some operations cannot be undone by a database rollback, because the earlier steps already committed in other systems. A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, each written to reverse an earlier step, is often called a saga. Its durable record tracks completed steps, unresolved operations, and required counteractions. Compensation follows business dependencies and the actions still available. For a parcel already dispatched, recovery may involve a return process.

When reviewing a multi-step operation, we can examine each point at which processing might end. Which completed actions would need compensation, which outcomes would require investigation, and where would that work be recorded? The answers define the recovery paths the application must support.

Events and the Transactional Outbox

A related recording problem appears when a service updates its database and publishes an event. Suppose Order Service commits an order transition, then stops before publishing the corresponding event. Downstream consumers receive no notification. Publishing first introduces another failure case, because the broker could accept the event and the database transaction could subsequently fail.

Both orders fail for the same reason: two separate systems cannot be updated in one step. An outbox keeps the unpublished event as a durable database record until a relay finds and publishes it (Figure Figure).

With a transactional outbox, Order Service writes the state change and an event record in the same database transaction. A separate relay publishes committed outbox records.

Here, advance validates the permitted transition, checks the expected version, and increments it. A rejected transition aborts the transaction, so it cannot produce an event claiming that the transition occurred. The relay marks an event as published after the broker acknowledges acceptance under the configured durability contract. An interruption between broker acceptance and that local update can cause the relay to publish the event again using the same message ID.

A consumer can handle repeated delivery by recording the message ID in the same database transaction as its business update.

Both repositories use the same transactional database, and the marker insertion uses a database uniqueness constraint to resolve concurrent deliveries. If the transaction fails, the marker and reservation update roll back together, and the message is not acknowledged. If the commit succeeds but acknowledgment is lost, another delivery finds the marker and avoids repeating the update.

The marker must cover the period during which the message may be replayed. The reservation also needs a business identity, since two distinct messages could request the same reservation. Their different message IDs would pass the delivery check.

If the consumer calls an external warehouse or payment provider, that provider’s commit falls outside the local transaction. The consumer then needs the operation record and recovery procedure discussed earlier.

Parallel relays can also publish successive order events in the wrong sequence. A workflow that depends on sequence needs per-order publication ordering or version checks with a defined response to gaps. We will examine those choices in Chapter 12.

The outbox gives Order Service a durable record of what must be published. Publication can be delayed by a process failure, and the relay can resume from the committed record.

Recovery in Production

Recovery is the one part of a system that looks identical whether it is working perfectly or not running at all, at least until a customer calls.

Durable records allow the team to measure unfinished work and investigate cases that automatic recovery cannot resolve. Baodium tracked unresolved operation count and the age of the oldest unresolved operation. After a provider outage, the engineers compared new unresolved operations with recovery completions to determine whether the backlog was decreasing.

Compensation had its own monitoring and escalation path, because an order could be marked canceled while its payment void was pending. The customer interface and support view distinguished those outcomes so neither implied that the payment had already been resolved.

The engineers also compared local and provider records in both directions. Starting from local operations revealed missing or conflicting provider results. Starting from provider records revealed authorizations with no matching local operation, including effects created by older or faulty code. Checking only provider IDs already stored locally could miss an authorization whose response had been lost.

Order IDs, operation IDs, provider references, and recovery history were available in logs and the operator view. Aggregate metrics reported unresolved age, conflicts, duplicate effects, and recovery outcomes. Individual identifiers were excluded from metric labels to avoid creating a separate time series for every order.

Operators used controlled recovery actions with the same rules as the application. A manual retry reused the stored operation and respected provider retention limits. A replacement authorization required an established outcome for the previous operation and a recorded business reason.

Before release, the engineers interrupted processing after intent commit, after provider acceptance, and after local result commit. They also tested concurrent submissions, late responses, expired recovery claims, and repeated event delivery. For each test, they inspected local records and provider effects. When a test lost the authorization response, recovery had to resolve the original operation without creating another authorization. The eventual HTTP response alone could not settle that question.

Summary

The customer who submitted a payment twice after receiving no confirmation exposed a gap between Baodium’s local records and the provider’s result. A timeout established that the caller had stopped waiting. It did not establish whether the provider had authorized the payment, rejected it, or was still processing it. Treating the timeout as a failure permitted a second authorization for the same purchase.

The repair begins before the outbound request. Baodium records a durable operation identity, then uses that identity across attempts and recovery. Once an authorization has been dispatched, an unanswered request moves into an explicit unresolved state. Reconciliation may establish the outcome; a repeated submission retrieves the existing operation instead of creating a new one. Guarded state transitions prevent delayed responses from replacing a later, verified result. Compensation and event publication require the same discipline when a workflow crosses additional systems.

An integration review should therefore include a failure immediately after the remote side effect. If the calling process stops at that point, another process must be able to find the operation, determine what evidence is authoritative, and continue without duplicating the action. Chapter 4 examines what happens to the workers, deadlines, and downstream calls while that first attempt is still in progress.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Repeated attempts for one authorization can be recognized through the provider’s documented idempotency and recovery mechanisms, subject to their scope and retention limits.
Condition that tests it & A response is lost or a delayed result arrives after another checkout update.
Constraint or invariant & Baodium and the payment provider commit separately. A local rollback cannot remove a provider authorization.
Evidence and uncertainty & The opening incident produced two authorizations after one response was lost. Recovery tests inspect provider effects as well as local records.

The outcome of an interrupted provider call, including requests still processing or no longer covered by duplicate recognition.
Signal and evaluation window & Track unresolved-operation age and compare local state with provider evidence during recovery.
Control and decision & Recover the existing operation while its outcome is unresolved. Permit a replacement authorization only after establishing the earlier outcome and checking that the business workflow permits another payment.
Owner and review trigger & The payment-service owner defines operation identity and recovery. Operations staff manage escalated cases through an audited procedure. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.
